narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who was accepted ranked around the 5.8th decile in their third year, you placed in the first decile, a substantial drop from your first-year performance where you matched the accepted-student average.

Your undergraduate GPA and LSAT score were the next two most important factors, though they pulled in opposite directions. Your GPA of 3.00 was slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students and modestly increased the predicted risk of failure. In contrast, your LSAT score of 28 was well below the accepted average of 37 and actually worked in your favor by lowering the chance of failure, but not enough to overcome the other signals.

Your family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, or enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program that can demonstrate a clear upward trend in grades before reapplying. (198 words)
